title: Learned per-run publish-push throughput for write speed and ETA
summary: Compute the dashboard 'Push file' write speed and ETA from a per-run weighted average of completed server-push throughput instead of the in-progress file's lifetime partial average, which read far below the real transfer rate early in a file.
reason: The displayed write speed used total-bytes-copied / total-elapsed for the in-progress file. Early in a multi-GB push the slow ramp-up dominates that average, so the operator saw ~13.5 MB/s while the link was actually moving ~50 MB/s. A completed file's full-transfer average is a far better predictor, so each finished server push now refines a session average that drives the speed and ETA for subsequent files.
behavior_before: The 'Push file' card showed write speed and ETA derived from the in-progress file's cumulative bytes/elapsed, which understated the rate (and overstated the ETA) while the transfer was still ramping up.
behavior_after: The copy-telemetry writer accumulates a per-run weighted average (sum bytes / sum seconds) of completed server pushes and emits CopySessionBytesPerSecond / CopySessionFilesCompleted. Once at least one file in the run has finished, eta.py uses that learned average for the current push's write speed and ETA; the first file of a run still falls back to its own partial measurement. The local source->scratch copy is excluded (it uses CopyState, not PushState), so fast local copies never pollute the network average. No copy, publish, queue, or media behavior changed.
